Its final ت is the feminine marker (tā' al-ta'nīth), not a root radical, so the word has no ordinary triliteral verbal root.

3.meaning: The splitting or cracking open — specifically the way the earth's surface splits apart as plants push up and water breaks through. The noun names the act/result of cleaving open. In the oath of 86:12, "the earth, possessor of splitting," it evokes soil that cracks open to bring forth vegetation, which is why it is rendered "sprouting plants."

parts.en: the
a splitting / cracking open
genitive ending (linking it to the preceding word)

3.grammar: A definite noun: the prefix الـ (al-) means "the," and the stem ṣadʿ names a splitting or cleaving open. (The doubling/shadda on the ص is just the "l" of al- assimilating into the solar letter ص when spoken — al-ṣadʿ → aṣ-ṣadʿ — not a separate part of the word.) The final ـِ (-i) is the genitive case (kasrah). It is genitive because the word follows ذَاتِ ("possessor of") in a possessive linkage (iḍāfa) — literally "the earth, possessor OF the splitting," i.e., the earth that cracks open. So the -i ending signals "OF…," tying this noun to the word before it.

1.meaning: A two-part word combining the emphatic particle "inna" with the pronoun "He." "Inna" has no clean English equivalent: it is a particle of emphasis and certainty placed at the head of a sentence to assert its truth strongly, conveying the force of "indeed," "surely," or "most certainly." The attached pronoun refers to Allah. Together the word declares with emphasis: "Indeed He / Surely He," opening a statement that affirms something about Allah with full conviction.

parts.en: indeed / surely (particle of emphasis and certainty)
He / Him (3rd-person masculine singular pronoun, here referring to Allah)

1.grammar: "Inna" is an emphasizing particle that introduces a nominal sentence and strongly affirms its content (like saying "it is truly the case that..."). Grammatically it governs what follows: the noun or pronoun after it takes the accusative as its "subject" (اسم إنَّ). The attached pronoun هٗ (-hu) is that subject in the accusative state, meaning "He" and referring to Allah, while the predicate ("is fully capable...") completes the emphatic claim. The pronoun appears here in its lengthened/rounded form -hū (marked by the small superscript wāw ٗ): this is the recited form the 3rd-masc-sg suffix takes after a fatha or damma, and here it follows the fatha on نَّ. (By contrast, after a kasra or yā' — an "i" environment — the same suffix becomes -hi, as in بِهِ bihi and فِيهِ fīhi.)
1.root: — (inna is a particle and has no triliteral root; -hu is a pronoun and has no root)

2.meaning: At its core this means "is surely a word/an utterance/a saying." The dominant element is قَوۡل (qawl), a verbal noun meaning a pronounced word, speech, or saying — here used of revealed divine speech (the Qur'an itself). The attached لَـ (la-) is the "emphatic lām," a prefix that carries no English word of its own but stresses and affirms what follows, like saying "is truly/most certainly a word." So the whole conveys emphatic affirmation: "it is indeed, beyond doubt, a [decisive] word."

parts.en: surely / indeed (emphatic prefix)
word, speech, saying
indefinite nominative ending ('a word')

2.grammar: This is a noun, not a verb. The opening لَـ (la-) is the emphatic lām: it adds force and certainty ("surely, truly") and typically appears in the predicate after the particle إِنَّ ("indeed"), as in inna-hu la-qawlun ("indeed it is surely a word"). The final ending is -un (nunation/tanwīn with ḍamma): the -u shows it is in the nominative case — it is the predicate (khabar) of إِنَّ, which takes the nominative, telling you what the subject "it" is — and the -n (nunation) marks it as indefinite, "a word," not "the word." So the ending says: indefinite + nominative, serving as the thing being affirmed about the subject.
2.root: ق-و-ل (q-w-l) — to say, to speak; an utterance or word

3.meaning: A decisive, final pronouncement that separates truth from falsehood and right from wrong — a word that settles a matter conclusively and is no idle jest. As a description of the Qur'an, it means speech that judges definitively, distinguishing the true from the false with no ambiguity.

parts.en: a decisive separation; a clear-cut, conclusive judgment
nominative indefinite ending ('a …')

3.grammar: This is a singular indefinite noun used here as a descriptive term (functioning like an adjective, 'decisive'). The final -un ending (the double-vowel 'tanwīn' ḍamma) marks two things at once: it is nominative case, because it describes the preceding noun qawl ('a word') — itself the predicate (xabar) of the emphatic particle inna and therefore nominative — and the tanwīn (the -n sound) signals that the noun is indefinite, 'a decisive [word]'. So the ending tells you it agrees with 'word' as its description and stands without 'the'.
3.root: ف-ص-ل (f-ṣ-l) — to separate, divide, distinguish; hence to judge decisively (the same root gives faṣl 'a clear distinction' and the idea of a final verdict that parts truth from falsehood)

1.meaning: A two-part particle cluster meaning "and not / and ... is not." It joins the clause to what precedes with "and" (wa-), then negates it with mā — a particle that denies a present-tense statement of fact, asserting that something is simply not the case. In 86:14 it states that the Qur'an "is not" frivolous speech.

parts.en: and (the shadda is a recitation/tajwid mark: the tanwīn ending the preceding word faṣlun assimilates into this waw — idghām with ghunnah — not an extra letter)
not (particle of negation)

1.grammar: Two indeclinable particles, so there is no case ending to parse. wa- is the connector "and." The shadda written on it is a Quranic recitation (tajwid) mark, not a separate letter and not an assimilation to the word that follows: the preceding word in 86:13–14 is faṣlun (فَصۡلٞ), which ends in tanwīn (an -n sound), and waw is one of the letters into which a tanwīn/nūn merges with nasalization (idghām bi-ghunnah); the mushaf records that merger as a shadda on the waw. mā is a negating particle: placed before a nominal sentence (as in 86:14, "and it is not to be taken lightly") it flatly denies the statement, equivalent to English "is not / does not." Because both are particles, nothing here inflects for person, number, or tense.

2.meaning: The standalone third-person masculine singular pronoun "he" or "it." It is the independent (detached) form of the pronoun, used as a subject standing on its own rather than attached to a verb or noun. Depending on what it refers back to, it can mean "he," "it," or — in equational (verbless) sentences — function like the linking verb "is" (e.g., "He is..." / "It is..."). In 86:14 it points back to the Qur'an: "and it [the Qur'an] is not to be taken lightly."

parts.en: he / it (independent 3rd-person masculine singular pronoun)

2.grammar: This is one indivisible word — a detached personal pronoun (ḍamīr munfaṣil), not built from a root with prefixes or endings. It is "mabnī" (indeclinable): its shape is permanently fixed, built on fatḥa, so the final "-a" vowel never changes for case and it reads the same whether it functions as subject, predicate, or object. It always refers to a single masculine (or grammatically masculine) entity. Standing alone like this, it most often serves as the subject of a sentence ("he/it ...") or as the linking "is" in a verbless (equational) sentence.
2.root: — (a primitive pronoun; it has no triliteral root)

3.meaning: A solemn negation of frivolity. Al-hazl is jest, joking, or idle amusement — speech meant for play rather than truth. In its context (86:14, "and it is not bil-hazl"), the Qur'an declares itself the opposite of hazl: it is decisive, serious truth (al-fasl, "the decisive word" of the preceding verse), not lighthearted banter or empty entertainment to be brushed aside.

parts.en: emphatic/redundant particle (ba zaidah). After the negation ma huwa ("it is not...") it carries no lexical meaning of its own; it simply intensifies the negation — roughly "it is not jest at all."
the (definite article; here gives a generic, whole-category sense — jest of any kind)
jest, joking, idle amusement

3.grammar: The core word is hazl, a masdar (verbal noun) from the verb hazala ("to jest, joke"), meaning the act or category of jesting. It is preceded by the definite article al- ("the"), which here lends a generic sense: jest of any kind. The whole is carried by the prefixed bi-. Crucially, this bi- is not the lexical preposition "with"; in the construction ma huwa bil-hazl it is the ba zaidah (the "redundant ba"), an emphatic particle that reinforces the negation without adding independent meaning — the sense is "it is not jest in the least." Grammatically, the ba zaidah still governs the genitive, so hazl takes the genitive -i ending (hazli), exactly as any noun after bi- must.
3.root: ه-ز-ل (h-z-l) — to jest, joke, speak in fun (the opposite of speaking in earnest, jidd)

1.meaning: A two-part word combining the emphasis particle "inna" with the pronoun "they." "Inna" has no clean English equivalent — it is a particle placed at the head of a sentence to affirm and strengthen the statement that follows, conveying the force of "indeed," "truly," or "it is certainly the case that." Together, "innahum" asserts emphatically: "Indeed they / truly they / they most certainly." It introduces a confident, settled declaration about the people in question. In 86:15 (اِنَّهُمۡ يَكِيۡدُوۡنَ كَيۡدًا) it carries the sense "They are certainly devising ˹evil˺ plans."

parts.en: indeed / truly (emphasis particle)
they / them (attached pronoun, 3rd person masculine plural)

1.grammar: "Inna" is an emphasis particle (ḥarf tawkīd wa-naṣb) that grammatically governs the noun or pronoun after it, placing it in the accusative ("naṣb") position. The attached pronoun "-hum" is that governed element — technically the ism inna (the "noun of inna"), which sits in the accusative case, NOT the nominative. It is the logical/semantic subject of the statement (the people the emphatic claim is about), but grammatically it functions as the accusative ism inna, not as a nominative subject (mubtadaʾ or fāʿil). The pronoun "-hum" is the 3rd-person masculine plural form (referring to a group of males, or a mixed/general group); like all attached pronouns it is indeclinable (mabnī) — its form "hum" stays fixed and does not inflect, so it occupies the accusative position without any visible case change. So the whole word means roughly "indeed they (are)…," with "inna" supplying the emphasis and "-hum" naming the people the emphatic claim concerns.
1.root: — (none — "inna" is a particle and "hum" is a pronoun; neither derives from a triliteral root)

2.meaning: They plot, scheme, and devise crafty stratagems. The verb describes the ongoing act of secretly contriving a plan or stratagem against someone — here, scheming against the truth and its Messenger. The present-tense form conveys continuous, repeated effort, so "they are plotting / they keep scheming."

parts.en: 3rd-person masculine imperfect (present-tense) prefix
plot / scheme (Form I imperfect stem; ī from the hollow root's medial ya')
they (masculine plural) + indicative mood marker

2.grammar: A Form I present-tense (imperfect) verb, third person masculine plural ("they"). It comes from a "hollow" root whose middle radical is ya', which surfaces in this form as the long vowel ī (yakīd-). The ya- prefix marks the third-person masculine imperfect, while number is shown by the ending: here -ūna is built from -ū ("they," masculine plural) plus -na, the marker of the indicative mood — telling us this is a plain factual statement ("they are plotting") rather than a wish or command. The imperfect aspect gives the sense of ongoing, repeated action.
2.root: ك-ي-د (k-y-d) — to plot, scheme, devise a (often crafty or hostile) stratagem

3.meaning: A scheme, plot, or cunning stratagem — a covert plan devised against someone, typically with hostile or malicious intent. It carries the sense of deceptive, calculated maneuvering: laying a trap or working in secret to undermine another. In context it is "evil planning" or "scheming."

parts.en: a plot, scheme, cunning stratagem
indefinite accusative ending ("a/an" + object case)

3.grammar: A masculine singular noun in the indefinite accusative case, shown by the final -an (the tanwīn fatḥah, written ـً). Here it is a "cognate accusative" (maf'ul mutlaq): the same root is repeated after its verb (yakīdūna kaydan, literally "they plot a plotting") to intensify and emphasize the action — "they scheme a mighty scheme" / "they plot relentlessly." The accusative ending marks it as the object/complement reinforcing the verb, not a separate thing being acted upon.
3.root: ك-ي-د (k-y-d) — plotting, scheming, devising a cunning plan

1.meaning: This is a conjunction joined to a verb meaning "and/but I am devising a plan." The verb carries the sense of working out a stratagem or quietly setting a scheme in motion against an opponent. In context (86:16) it follows the statement that the disbelievers scheme — so Allah declares that He too is putting a plan into effect, one that will decisively outmatch theirs. The continuous present sense ("I am planning") conveys an ongoing, deliberate response.

parts.en: and / but (connecting word; written with a shadda because the -an ending of the previous word كَيۡدًا merges into this waw in recitation)
I (the 'a-' prefix on a present-tense verb marks the first-person singular 'I')
am planning / scheming (present-tense verb stem)

1.grammar: A present/imperfect (ongoing) verb in the first person singular: the a- prefix means "I," giving "I plan / I am planning." The final -u ending is the indicative mood marker — it signals a plain factual statement ("I do/am doing this"), as opposed to a command or a negated/subjunctive form. The opening wa- is the connector "and/but"; it carries a shadda (doubling) because of a tajwid rule called idgham: the tanwin (the -an "nunation" sound) at the end of the preceding word كَيۡدًا assimilates into this waw. The waw is the recipient of the merging — the preceding nūn-sound flows into it — which is why the waw, not the previous word, takes the shadda. Root form I verb, simple and direct in meaning.
1.root: ك-ي-د (k-y-d) — to plan, scheme, or devise a stratagem (often a covert plot or counter-plot)

2.meaning: A scheme, plot, or cunning stratagem — a covert plan devised against someone, typically with hostile or malicious intent. It carries the sense of deceptive, calculated maneuvering: laying a trap or working in secret to undermine another. In context it is "evil planning" or "scheming."

parts.en: a plot, scheme, cunning stratagem
indefinite accusative ending ("a/an" + object case)

2.grammar: A masculine singular noun in the indefinite accusative case, shown by the final -an (the tanwīn fatḥah, written ـً). Here it is a "cognate accusative" (maf'ul mutlaq): the same root is repeated after its verb (yakīdūna kaydan, literally "they plot a plotting") to intensify and emphasize the action — "they scheme a mighty scheme" / "they plot relentlessly." The accusative ending marks it as the object/complement reinforcing the verb, not a separate thing being acted upon.
2.root: ك-ي-د (k-y-d) — plotting, scheming, devising a cunning plan

1.meaning: A command meaning "so grant them respite" / "so bear with them, give them time." The Form II verb conveys letting someone be and not rushing them, allowing a period of delay before a reckoning. In 86:17 it is an instruction to the Prophet to be patient with the disbelievers and give them a little more time.

parts.en: so / then (connective prefix)
grant respite! / give (them) time! (command, addressed to one male)

1.grammar: This is a Form II (taf'īl) command (imperative) verb addressed to a single male ("you, grant respite!"). Form II doubles the middle root letter (mahhala) and gives an intensive/causative force: from the idea of slowness it means "to grant a delay, let be." The verb's own underlying ending is a silent sukūn (mahhil). The final kasra you see (mahhili) is NOT a case or mood ending and is NOT a separate element: it is a helping vowel (kasrat al-waṣl, the kasra of liaison) added to the verb's own final consonant because the next word begins with the article الـ (al-), whose connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) drops in continuous speech. A consonant cannot link onto that, so a kasra is inserted to ease pronunciation: mahhil → mahhili l-kāfirīn. The fa- prefix simply links this command to what precedes ("so...").
1.root: م-ه-ل (m-h-l) — slowness, unhurried delay; granting time/respite

2.meaning: "The disbelievers / the ones who reject faith" — referring to people who cover over and refuse the truth of Allah and His signs. The underlying image (from the root k-f-r) is of someone who "covers up" or "buries" the truth — concealing what they have been shown and being ungrateful for Allah's favors, hence willfully rejecting belief. The definite article ("the") points to a known group of such rejecters, whether a specific set of people or the class in general.

parts.en: the (definite article)
disbeliever / one who covers over and rejects the truth (active participle)
masculine sound plural ending, oblique case (accusative/genitive)

2.grammar: A sound masculine plural noun — an active participle ("the rejecters / disbelievers") — made definite by the article al-. The ending is ـِينَ (-īna), not ـُونَ (-ūna): the -īna form marks the oblique case, used when the word is a direct object (accusative) or governed by a preposition or possessive (genitive). In 86:17 it is the accusative direct object of the Form II imperative فَمَهِّلِ (famahhil, "so grant respite to / bear with") — the disbelievers are the ones being acted upon by the command. Had it been the subject, it would read al-kāfirūna with -ūna.
2.root: ك-ف-ر (k-f-r) — to cover over, conceal; hence to reject faith / be ungrateful, to disbelieve

3.meaning: A command meaning "grant them respite" / "give them more time" / "bear with them a little." It is an order to the Prophet (peace be upon him) to leave the disbelievers be for now — to be patient with them and not press for their punishment, granting them a delay or reprieve. The sense carries gentleness and unhurried forbearance rather than mere passive waiting.

parts.en: grant respite! / give a delay! — Form IV imperative (2nd person masculine singular). The initial اَ (hamzat al-qaṭʿ with fatḥa) is built into the Form IV pattern أَفۡعِلۡ and is not a detachable prefix.
them (attached object pronoun, masculine plural)

3.grammar: This is a Form IV command (imperative) addressed to a single 'you' (the Prophet), the imperative of the verb أَمۡهَلَ. Its base أَمۡهِلۡ follows the Form IV imperative pattern أَفۡعِلۡ. The opening أَ is hamzat al-qaṭʿ (a proper, non-eliding hamza) carrying fatḥa, and it is an intrinsic part of the Form IV binyan (وزن أَفۡعَلَ) — not a separable imperative marker and not hamzat al-waṣl. (Hamzat al-waṣl in imperatives carries kasra and belongs to Forms I, VII, VIII and X, e.g. اِكۡتُبۡ; it never takes fatḥa here.) Form IV (أَفۡعَلَ) typically makes a verb causative, so the root sense of slowness/gentleness becomes "to grant someone time, to let them be." The verb ends in a silent sukūn on the lām (amhil, no case vowel) — this jussive-form, vowel-less ending is what marks it as a command ("give respite!") rather than a statement. The attached هُمۡ (-hum) is the direct object 'them', so the whole word means "grant-respite-to-them." It pairs with the parallel command مَهِّلۡ (mahhil, Form II) in the same ayah for emphasis.

4.meaning: An adverb meaning "a little," "just a short while," or "gently/slowly." It is the diminutive (by truncation) of irwad, the verbal noun of the Form IV verb arwada ("to act gently, go easy, take one's time"), from the root meaning "to be gentle, easy, unhurried." The diminutive shrinks the sense to "a tiny bit," so it conveys "for just a brief moment" or "ever so gently." In 86:17 it tells the Prophet to grant the disbelievers only the briefest respite -- a measured, fleeting delay before the reckoning comes.

parts.en: a little / gently (truncated diminutive of the verbal noun 'irwad')
accusative '-an' ending (tanwin); marks the cognate/adverbial accusative

4.grammar: The word has two well-established grammatical identities. (1) On its own, رويد is an ism fi'l amr -- a noun that stands in place of an imperative verb -- meaning "go gently, take it easy, hold on." (2) With the accusative tanwin (the "-an" written with the alif), as here (ruwaydan), it functions as a maf'ul mutlaq: a cognate/absolute accusative that stands in for the verbal noun (masdar) of the action, reinforcing the command "let them be" with the sense "...for just a little while" or "...gently." Morphologically رويد is a diminutive on the pattern fu'ayl. The authoritative view (Sibawayhi) is that it is a TRUNCATED diminutive (tasghir al-tarkhim) of irwad -- the masdar of the Form IV verb arwada -- not of the simple noun rud/rawd (which is the minority view Sibawayhi criticized, since rud does not stand in the position of a verb the way irwad does). The diminutive shrinks the meaning to "just a tiny bit," and the "-an" ending matches the transliteration ruwaydan.
4.root: ر-و-د (r-w-d) -- to go gently, seek without haste, move at ease
